title: Sequence-conditioned CogMol designs SARS-CoV-2 spike and main-protease inhibitors
summary: IBM Research and academic collaborators used the CogMol deep generative foundation model to design compounds from target protein sequence information alone for SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain and main protease. In vitro inhibition was reported for two of four synthesized candidates for each target; the most potent spike-RBD inhibitor also showed activity against multiple variants in live-virus neutralization assays.
ai_technology: CogMol, a sequence-conditioned deep generative foundation model using a molecular variational autoencoder and protein–ligand binding predictor
organization: IBM Research; Diamond Light Source; University of Oxford; Enamine Ltd.; associated research centers

evidence.tested: In vitro inhibition was reported for two of four synthesized candidates for each target; the most potent spike-RBD inhibitor also showed activity against multiple variants in live-virus neutralization assays.
evidence.unknown: The source describes a proof of concept with a small selected synthesis set from roughly 100 ranked designs. Only in-vitro target assays were performed; the leading RBD inhibitor was also tested in live-virus neutralization against variants. The paper says ADME attributes were not experimentally validated and further work is needed to confirm inhibitor binding mechanisms. These are preclinical leads, not medicines or demonstrated clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: The team sampled CogMol conditioned on each target's amino-acid sequence to generate candidate small molecules; candidates were filtered and ranked in silico, synthesized and assayed. The model generated compounds without target-specific fine-tuning or target-structure input at inference; assays found micromolar inhibition for 2/4 synthesized candidates for each target.
